name: Natqgu
confidence_why: Boerger's 2022 grammar sketch, the fullest description of Natügu and the product of decades of fieldwork, gives fixed penultimate stress with quantity-insensitive trochaic feet, whereas Wurm (1969, 1970, 1976) only hedged that stress "may be phonemic" and de la Fontinelle (1974) claimed for the Néo dialect that the accent can fall on any syllable, yet her own examples and wordlist are almost all…

Port Moresby: Linguistic Society of Papua New Guinea, LLM 'Texts in the Indigenous Languages of the Pacific' (TILP) 2020-2023 collection. 71 pp. Open PDF: https://www.langlxmelanesia.com/_files/ugd/4bb486_7e4e85dfaba047998caf2a3c50be1c28.pdf
catalog_locator: §2.3 Stress, p. 4 (PDF page 4 = printed page 4; text layer); supporting derivation §2.5 Rule 4, p. 6 (PDF page 6, text); syllabification remark §2.1, p. 4 (line 165-166)
catalog_quote: Natqgu, like most Oceanic languages, exhibits stress on the penultimate mora of a syllable. Single morphemes have been identified with from one to six syllables. Most roots are comprised of one, two or three syllables. Primary stress remains penultimate in multisyllabic complex words. The placement of secondary stress correlates with the basic foot type found in Natügu. Beyond one-syllable words the foot type is a syllabic trochee. That is, feet are left headed and quantity insensitive. ... For example, vz-tr-mq |go-GDIR.in-PDIR.hither| ‘come in’ becomes [vztrpʰ] with stress on trpʰ. That is, penultimate stress is assigned, rule two applies, then rule 4 deletes [q], leaving stress where it originally occurred.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate mora/syllable of the word, including morphologically complex words (the author's phrase 'penultimate mora of a syllable' is evidently 'of the word'); feet are left-headed syllabic trochees, quantity-insensitive, so secondary stresses fall on alternate syllables leftward from the primary. Rule 4 (p. 7) shows stress is assigned before word-final /q/ [y] deletion, so a surface form like [vztrpʰ] 'come in' keeps stress on what was the penult.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated: 'The placement of secondary stress correlates with the basic foot type.. a syllabic trochee.. feet are left headed and quantity insensitive.' No examples given.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; §2.1 notes that a second vowel of a VV sequence that must bear stress is syllabified separately, and §2.5 Rule 4 notes surface final stress after word-final q-deletion in fast speech. Older source Wurm 1969: 60 / 1970: 477 / 1976: 643 said stress only partly predictable and 'may be phonemic'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (single morphemes and multisyllabic complex words, i.e. the verb complex); no phrase-level statement; no instrumental data; sketch draws on the Bznwz-village variety area of Graciosa Bay.
new_statements.identity_note: Boerger 2022 describes Natqgu/Natügu [ntu] = natu1246 as spoken in the Graciosa Bay villages of Santa Cruz Island (Bznwz variety identified as highest status). Wurm's 1969/1970/1976 'Malo' communalect = Northern Santa Cruz = Natügu (natu1246); his 'Nea', 'Nemboi/Menjembelo' and 'Nooli' = Nalögo (nalo1234) and 'Nanggu' = Engdewu (nang1262). de la Fontinelle 1974 describes the Néo (Tömotu Neo) dialect, assigned to natu1246 by Glottolog but not verified here. Boerger 2022 is a 71-page sketch; Glottolog's '306 pp' evidently counts the companion Meabr autobiography volumes in the same TILP collection.

new_statements.quote: L'accent : L'accent peut frapper n'importe quelle syllabe du mot. Ainsi : nény (vent), møréa (village), dá-kæ-nǿ-ŋy (la nourriture, la chose qui se mange) : c'est dans ce dernier cas l'article qui est accentué : ŋy (manger, terme poli) précédé de l'article nǿ-ŋy (le manger), da reçoit un accent secondaire. Dans tœ-mámi (le volcan), c'est l'élément lexical qui est mis en valeur par rapport à l'outil grammatical, dont il est d'ailleurs inséparable.
new_statements.translation: Accent: The accent can fall on any syllable of the word. Thus: nény 'wind', møréa 'village', dá-kæ-nǿ-ŋy 'the food, the thing that is eaten': in this last case it is the article that is accented: ŋy 'to eat (polite term)' preceded by the article, nǿ-ŋy 'the eating'; da receives a secondary accent. In tœ-mámi 'the volcano', it is the lexical element that is given prominence relative to the grammatical tool, from which it is moreover inseparable.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog records fixed penultimate stress (Boerger 2022, §2.3: primary stress penultimate, quantity-insensitive trochee). De la Fontinelle 1974 claims for the Néo dialect that the accent can fall on any syllable and treats it as distinctive, i.e. a different type (free/lexical rather than fixed penultimate). The contradiction is weak in the data: all four of her illustrative words and most of her stress-marked wordlist are penultimate; only a few forms (næl'vyn, na'bæ, ve'i, ma'i, nambæ-'lwæ) are final-stressed, and those involve hiatus vowel sequences or compounds. Her statement resembles Wurm 1969 p. 60 ('stress may be phonemic'), which Boerger's later full description supersedes.
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the Néo dialect (1972 data from one speaker, a few days of elicitation) the author states that the accent can strike any syllable of the word and gives no placement rule; accent is treated as distinctive (p. 285: two accentual types CV'V vs 'CVV, e.g. mwœ = /mu+œ/ vs lúv; p. 293: 'L'accent permet d'identifier la frontière entre l'outil et la racine'). In the stress-marked Néo wordlist (pp. 296-297) most polysyllables are nonetheless penultimate ('noblo, 'nelæ, i'roro, na'lœpy, bɔ'ŋavæ, æsi'kapu, lø'pøki), with a handful of final-stressed forms (næl'vyn '5', na'bæ 'shoulder', ve'i 'star', ma'i 'morning', nambæ-'lwæ 'valley'), several involving vowel sequences or compounds.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned once: in dá-kæ-nǿ-ŋy 'the food' the first element da carries a secondary accent while the article nǿ- carries the primary one (pp. 288-289). No general rule for secondary stress is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Classifier/article prefixes are described as accented or unaccented lexically (no- 'plant classifier' unaccented, né- 'part of a whole' accented, pp. 293-294); long vowels are analysed as accent on the first mora of a sequence of identical vowels (loo 'sago palm', p. 288); diphthongs ei are attributed to accent placement (blémei, néinø, p. 288).
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes the Néo dialect, spoken in the village of Néo on the north-west coast of Tömotu Neo (the island the author calls 'île de Malo'), from a single speaker (Margaret Worek, née Inaglai) recorded in the New Hebrides in 1972. Wurm 1969 (p. 60, saved file wurm1969_PL-A21) places Tomotu Neo inside the Nambakaengo (= Northern Santa Cruz = Natügu, natu1246) language area, and de la Fontinelle herself treats Néo and Wurm's Malo as two dialects of one language, so the work is about natu1246, dialect Néo rather than Boerger's Bznwz/Malo varieties.

readall_conflicts: De la Fontinelle 1974 (Néo dialect, one informant, brief 1972 elicitation) states that the accent can fall on any syllable of the word and analyses it as contrastive (CV'V vs 'CVV), which conflicts in type with the catalog's fixed penultimate stress from Boerger 2022 (a full grammar sketch after decades of fieldwork). The earlier Wurm 1969/1970/1976 remarks already held by the project ('stress may be phonemic, though some features of the stress pattern are predictable') sit on the same side as de la Fontinelle. However, de la Fontinelle's own examples (nény, møréa, dá-kæ-nǿ-ŋy, tœ-mámi) and the great majority of her stress-marked wordlist are penultimate, so her data do not actually establish free placement; the exceptions are final-stressed forms with vowel hiatus or compound structure (ve'i, ma'i, na'bæ, næl'vyn, nambæ-'lwæ), which a mora- or morpheme-sensitive penultimate rule could absorb. The catalog's fixed: penultimate syllable reading stands; the 1974 statement is best logged as an early, tentative free-accent claim for the Néo dialect.
